standard.title: Language empowers relationships and roles
standard.description: recognise how language empowers relationships and roles
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how language expresses and creates personal and social identities (AC9E7LA01). They have not yet examined how language functions as a mechanism of power within communities — shaping membership, authority and social roles.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise how specific language choices empower or constrain relationships and define roles within communities.

nodes.label: Community membership through language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify language features that signal membership in specific communities, such as family registers, teen slang, technical jargon and classroom interaction patterns.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of community-specific language and explain how they signal belonging to that community.
nodes.typical_width: Compare language features across three or more communities (e.g. family, peer group, classroom), explaining how each signals membership and reinforces shared identity.
wider: Analyse how online community language (gaming, fandoms, professional forums) constructs hierarchies of expertise through jargon and access
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use language, including specific greetings in language, to reinforce relationships to Country/Place and community
Investigate how code-switching between community registers positions speakers differently depending on context

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate all informal language as equivalent; examining different community types reveals that the empowering function varies — jargon in professional contexts differs qualitatively from intimacy markers in family contexts. More community contexts resolve this flattening.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Language-community analysis is rich for Y9 students: the elaborations name First Nations language contexts alongside mainstream communities, offering genuinely different analytical lenses. Advancing students can explore how language both includes and excludes, and why community-specific language is a form of social capital.
success_criteria: Student identifies at least two community-specific language features and names the community each belongs to
Student explains how each language feature signals membership or reinforces belonging in that community

nodes.label: Language and power in roles
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise how language choices define and reinforce roles — such as authority, expertise or solidarity — within and across communities.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a role (e.g. teacher, expert, parent) and explain how specific language features construct or reinforce that role in a given text or interaction.
nodes.typical_width: Compare how language constructs authority versus solidarity roles across two or more contexts, explaining how choices position speakers relative to others.
wider: Analyse how the same speaker shifts language to assert or defer authority depending on audience and setting
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use language to assert cultural authority and knowledge in ways that resist mainstream framing
Investigate how gendered or age-related language norms empower some roles and constrain others

response_modes.reason: The link between language choice and power is abstract — students need scaffolded reasoning to move from observing a language feature to explaining how it constitutes power rather than merely describing it.

nodes.hinge_reason: The conceptual move from 'this is a language feature' to 'this feature constitutes power' is prerequisite for N3. Without it, students at N3 cannot explain empowerment as a mechanism — they can only describe features, not explain how those features make power.
success_criteria: Student identifies specific language features (e.g. imperative mode, technical register, terms of address) that construct a role
Student explains how those features empower or position the speaker in relation to others in that context

nodes.label: Language empowerment as a mechanism
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise how language choices function as mechanisms of empowerment — not just markers of identity — actively shaping relationships and roles rather than simply reflecting them.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how a specific language choice in a text actively constructs or reinforces a relationship dynamic, rather than merely describing it.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a text (e.g. a speech, social media post, classroom exchange) and explain how multiple language choices work together to empower particular roles or relationships, using metalanguage appropriately.
wider: Compare how the same relationship is constructed differently across two texts from different cultural or historical contexts
Analyse how First Nations Australian language use in literature creates empowerment through connection to Country and cultural knowledge, rather than through dominance
Examine how disrupting expected language norms can challenge established power relationships

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate understanding of community membership, role construction and the active/constitutive function of language into a single analytical move. The integration — language doesn't just reflect power, it creates it — is the core insight of the descriptor.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The constitutive view of language (language makes things happen rather than just describes them) is genuinely enriching territory for Year 9. Advancing students can engage with critical discourse analysis concepts — how language naturalises power relations — without being accelerated into senior content.
success_criteria: Student explains how a language choice actively constructs a relationship or role, not merely reflects it
Student uses appropriate metalanguage (e.g. register, mode, positioning) in their explanation
